warmup.q: A worker thread runs while (!stop) { spins++; }. One second later, main sets the plain field stop = true. What happens on a normal JDK 25 run?
options: The worker stops within a few nanoseconds
The worker stops within a millisecond or so, once the CPU cache is flushed
warmup.why: The JIT compiler, the part of the JVM that turns busy code into fast machine code, may read stop once. It keeps the value in a register and turns the loop into while (true). Nothing in the code tells it that another thread writes that field. The cache story in the second option is the tempting one, but caches keep each other up to date on their own. The value that goes stale is the copy the compiled code keeps in a register.

opening:
In an office, the manager writes "time to go home" on the whiteboard by the door, and everyone glances at the board now and then.

A program can do the same. A thread, one path of work running beside others in the same program, loops through small jobs and checks a shared field, stop, before each one. To make it finish, the main thread sets stop = true.

One day the field is set, and the worker keeps going, forever. No exception, no error: just a busy processor and a program that won't quit.

The code looks too simple to be wrong, and on one thread it isn't. Worse, one print line in the loop usually hides the bug, so it survives every quick test.

Testing and debugging ended with a question: how can one thread miss a write that another made long ago? In this lesson, we'll make the loop hang and find where the old value really lives (not where most people look). We'll catch the processor running two lines out of order, and meet the Java Memory Model, the rules for what one thread is promised about another's writes. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with an office that writes "time to go home" on the board, and a worker that never looked up. The board was never the problem. The caches agreed, and the store buffer delivered its note within nanoseconds. The worker was reading its notepad, a register the JIT chose for it, and volatile took the notepad away.

Now search your own code, or an open-source project, for loops that end on a flag, such as while (running) or while (!stop). If that field isn't volatile or an AtomicBoolean, the loop works only until the JIT notices.

Next, we'll read the rest of the rulebook: what links two threads in general, and what exactly is the promise called happens-before?

sections.h: The stop flag that never arrives: a plain field in a busy loop
sections.html:
Let's start with the smallest program that shows the bug. A worker thread counts in a loop, and each spins++ stands in for one small job. main starts the worker, waits one second, then sets the flag. Both versions do the same three things:

Java
static boolean stop;   // plain field

Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
    long spins = 0;
    while (!stop) {
        spins++;       // stands in for one small job
    }
    System.out.println("worker saw stop");
});
worker.start();
Thread.sleep(1_000);
stop = true;           // main asks the worker to stop
Kotlin
var stop = false       // plain property

val worker = thread {
    var spins = 0L
    while (!stop) {
        spins++        // stands in for one small job
    }
    println("worker saw stop")
}
Thread.sleep(1_000)
stop = true            // main asks the worker to stop

In Kotlin, thread { } creates the thread and starts it for us. In the demo, stop is a top-level var, which compiles to a plain static field, just like Java's.

Before you read on, decide what you expect. I'd expect worker saw stop a moment after main sets the flag. Here's what StopFlagDemo, the same program in the labs, printed on JDK 25 (JDK 21 does the same):

main set stop = true
worker still running 3 s later? true

The worker never stopped, and it wouldn't have stopped an hour later either. main wrote true, and the worker kept reading false. Nothing crashed and nothing complained. The worker just kept doing laps.

Let's change one thing and run the same file with java -Xint. That flag turns off the JIT compiler (the just-in-time compiler). The JIT is the part of the JVM, the program that runs your Java code, that turns code which runs often into fast machine code while the program runs. Without it, the JVM's interpreter carries out the bytecode, the simple instructions that javac turns your code into, one at a time, slowly and literally:

main set stop = true
worker saw stop after 113,153,939 spins
worker still running 3 s later? false

The worker stopped at once. Same machine, same processor, same memory. Only the JIT changed, so that's where the bug lives.

Here's what the JIT did. Once the loop had run many thousands of times, C2, the optimizing compiler inside HotSpot (the JVM in the standard JDK), compiled it. C2 saw that nothing in the loop writes stop or talks to other threads. So it read stop once, before the loop, kept the value in a register, and ran the rest as while (true). A register is a tiny storage slot inside a core, the part of the processor that runs one thread at a time. It's the fastest place a value can live.

A picture helps here, and we'll build on it all lesson. The office whiteboard holds the numbers everyone shares: that's memory. Each clerk also keeps a notepad on the desk. To work with a number, a clerk copies it onto the notepad, because a glance down is quicker than a walk to the wall. A register is that notepad. The compiled loop copied "stop: no" onto its notepad once, and has read only the notepad ever since. Nobody else can write on it, so no change on the board will ever reach it.

Whether, and when, one thread sees another thread's write is called visibility. The Java Memory Model (JMM), the part of the Java rules that settles it, promises visibility only when something links the two threads: a volatile field, a lock, Thread.join() and a few more you'll meet in the next lesson. A plain field has no link, so the compiler may assume that no other thread ever changes it.

The fix is one word:

Java
static volatile boolean stop;
Kotlin
@Volatile var stop = false

volatile is a keyword that marks a field as shared between threads. The JIT may not keep a volatile field on the notepad, so every pass of the loop reads it again. And the JMM promises that the write from main becomes visible to the loop. Kotlin's @Volatile annotation marks the compiled field volatile, so the bytecode is the same.

A plain field shared between threads comes with no promise. Make it volatile, or link the threads some other way.

The fix was easy. The odd part is that the JIT was allowed to break our loop at all, and that one print line would have hidden the damage. That's next.

steps: Read StopFlagDemo below (Java or Kotlin). Write down your guess: will the worker print worker saw stop?
Run it from labs/ with the Gradle command below. It waits 3 seconds for the worker, then exits.

Run the Java file again with the JIT turned off: java -Xint jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l01/StopFlagDemo.java (from labs/). That command runs a single Java source file directly, so it has no Kotlin version. The Kotlin twin compiles to the same field read, so the result carries over.
Make the field static volatile boolean stop; (in the Kotlin twin, write @Volatile private var stop = false) and run the Gradle command again.

code.title: StopFlagDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l01; /** A worker spins until main sets a plain boolean. Does it ever notice? */ public class StopFlagDemo { static boolean stop; // plain field: no volatile, no lock public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { long spins = 0; while (!stop) { spins++; } System.out.printf("worker saw stop after %,d spins%n", spins); }); worker.setDaemon(true); // so the JVM can exit even if the worker never stops worker.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); // give the JIT time to compile the loop stop = true; System.out.println("main set stop = true"); worker.join(3_000); System.out.println("worker still running 3 s later? " + worker.isAlive()); } }

alt.title: StopFlagDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.jmm.l01 import kotlin.concurrent.thread private var stop = false // plain field: no @Volatile, no lock /** A worker spins until main sets a plain boolean. Does it ever notice? */ fun main() { // daemon, so the JVM can exit even if the worker never stops val worker = thread(isDaemon = true) { var spins = 0L while (!stop) { spins++ } println("worker saw stop after %,d spins".format(spins)) } Thread.sleep(1_000) // give the JIT time to compile the loop stop = true println("main set stop = true") worker.join(3_000) println("worker still running 3 s later? ${worker.isAlive}") }

try.expect: The first run prints main set stop = true and then worker still running 3 s later? true. With -Xint, the worker prints how many times it spun, and stops, because the interpreter reads the field on every pass. With volatile, the compiled loop stops too, a moment after main sets the flag.

aside.title: Doesn't volatile make the loop slow?
aside.html: It's a fair worry: the loop now reads the field on every pass. With volatile on JDK 25, the worker spun about 2.1 billion times in its one second of work before main set the flag. The interpreter run above managed about 113 million. On x86 processors, a volatile read compiles to an ordinary read of memory, and the core's cache usually answers it in about a nanosecond. What volatile takes away is the JIT's freedom to skip the read, not the speed of the read itself.

sections.h: What the JIT may change: anything one thread alone can't notice
sections.html:
So why was C2 allowed to read stop only once? Every optimizer in the JVM follows one rule, often called as-if-serial: it may change your code in any way it likes, as long as a single thread running that code alone can't tell the difference.

A kitchen makes the rule easy to picture. A waiter's ticket for one table says soup, then salad. The cook makes the salad first, because it takes one minute and the soup takes ten, and the table gets both dishes. The people at the table can't tell the difference. Only a waiter watching the pass, the shelf where finished plates wait, sees the salad come out first. The cook promised the dishes on the ticket, not the order in which they're made.

In a program, the thread that runs the code is the table, and every other thread is the waiter at the pass. Reading stop once keeps the cook's promise. If no other thread existed, stop couldn't change during the loop, and the loop would behave exactly as written. Here is the change C2 is allowed to make, side by side:

// what you wrote             // what the compiled code may do
while (!stop) {               if (!stop) {
    spins++;                      while (true) { spins++; }
}                             }

Moving a read out of a loop like that is called hoisting. The same rule lets the JIT merge two writes to the same field into one, drop a write that nothing reads, or swap two writes to different fields. The thread that runs the code never notices. Another thread, reading those fields at the same time, can see every one of these changes.

The kitchen picture stops at one point. A cook decides plate by plate. The JIT decides once, when it compiles the loop, and the core then repeats that choice billions of times. That's why the hang is permanent, not a delay.

Now for the part that lets these bugs survive a code review, where teammates read each other's code before it ships. Put almost any method call inside the loop, and the hang usually goes away: Thread.sleep(10), a log line, Thread.yield(), even Thread.onSpinWait(). With Thread.yield(), a hint that the thread may give up its core for a moment, the demo stopped at once on JDK 25:

worker saw stop after 3,603,541 spins

C2 can't see inside a call like that, so it assumes the call might have changed any field, and it reads stop again afterwards. That's luck, not a promise. The Java Language Specification (JLS), the official rulebook of the language, says plainly that sleep and yield have no synchronization effect, meaning they link no threads. The compiler needn't even reload the values it keeps in registers after them. A later JDK might see inside more calls, or a teammate might swap the log line for a counter, and the hang comes back. A loop that has worked for two years is still broken. It just hasn't been compiled the wrong way yet.

A loop that stops by luck is still broken. Look for the link between the threads, not for the symptom.

So the JIT may rearrange our code, as long as one thread can't tell. Surely the processor, at least, runs exactly what it's given? Not quite, and that's where the office picture comes back.

try.title: Hide the bug without fixing it
steps: In StopFlagDemo (either language), take volatile or @Volatile off again, so the flag is plain.
Add Thread.yield() as the first line inside the while loop. Predict before you run: will the worker stop?
Run the Gradle command from the previous Try it.
try.expect: The worker stops. Thread.yield() ends in a call into the JVM that the JIT can't see inside, so the compiled code reads stop again after each call. The program is still wrong by the JMM: nothing promises that second read. Undo the change and keep volatile.

sections.h: Where the old value really lives: caches, store buffers and registers
sections.html:
The usual story about the stop flag goes like this: each core keeps its own copy of stop in its cache, that copy goes stale, and the worker reads it forever. A cache is a small, fast memory next to each core that keeps copies of recently used data. Main memory, the RAM, is about a hundred times slower. Each core has a small cache of its own, called L1, and the cores usually share a bigger one, often called L3.

The cache is where most people look, and the -Xint run already proved it wrong: the caches were the same in both runs, and only one run hung. Let's add caches to the office and see why.

Say each desk keeps a photocopy of the part of the whiteboard its clerk uses, so nobody has to walk to the wall. That's a cache. The office also has one strict rule: when anyone changes a number on the board, every photocopy of that number is crossed out at once, and the next look goes back to the board. Processors follow that rule in hardware, and it's called cache coherence. When one core writes a memory location, the other cores' copies are marked invalid or updated, usually within nanoseconds. No cache keeps an old value forever. The notepad has no such rule, which is why the compiled loop hung.

The hardware does have one place where a write can wait: the store buffer. Picture an outbox tray on each desk. When a clerk has a new number for the board, she drops the note in her tray and goes on to her next task. A runner carries it to the board a moment later. If her next task is to read a different number from the board, she may read it before her own note arrives. To everyone else, her write and her read look swapped.

A store buffer is that tray: a small queue inside each core where writes wait on their way to the cache, so the core can keep running. Here's the classic test for it. Two threads share two fields, x and y, which both start at 0:

Java
// thread A          // thread B
x = 1;               y = 1;
r1 = y;              r2 = x;
Kotlin
// thread A          // thread B
x = 1                y = 1
r1 = y               r2 = x

Before you look at the result, play the four lines by hand. Mix the two threads any way you like, but keep each thread's two lines in their order. It's like shuffling two decks of cards together without changing the order inside either deck. Whichever thread reads second runs after the other thread's write, so at least one thread reads a 1. Both reading 0 should be impossible.

ReorderDemo runs this test 524,288 times with plain fields, then again with volatile fields. One run on a 4-core machine printed:

run 1: both read 0 in 240,989 trials with plain fields, 0 with volatile fields (of 524,288)
run 2: both read 0 in 225,261 trials with plain fields, 0 with volatile fields (of 524,288)
run 3: both read 0 in 171,281 trials with plain fields, 0 with volatile fields (of 524,288)

The impossible result came up in a third to nearly half of the trials. Each thread's write was still in its own tray when it read the other field. With both fields volatile, it never happened. The JMM forbids that result for volatile fields, so on x86 processors HotSpot follows each volatile write with an instruction that empties the store buffer before any later read.

So here is the office as it stands. The photocopies, the caches, always agree within nanoseconds. The outbox tray, the store buffer, holds a write for a few nanoseconds and then always delivers it. The notepad, the register, can hold an old value forever, but only because the JIT chose to work from it. The picture breaks in one place: in the office, each clerk decides where to look. In the machine, the JIT chose the notepad once, when it compiled the loop, and the core never looks up again.

Processors also differ in how much they reorder. x86 processors, the kind in most laptops and servers, only let a later read pass an earlier write, as in the test above. ARM processors, which run phones, Apple Silicon Macs and many cloud servers, also let reads pass reads and writes pass writes. Code that never fails on an x86 laptop can fail on an ARM server.

The JIT and the processor have both rearranged our code now. Do you need to know what each of them does, on every machine, to write correct code? Happily, no.

try.title: Catch the processor reordering
steps: Read ReorderDemo (either language). It runs the two-thread test above 524,288 times with plain fields, then with volatile fields.
Run it with the Gradle command below and note the counts.
Run the Java file in the interpreter: java -Xint jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l01/ReorderDemo.java (from labs/). Predict first: the JIT is off now, so will the plain count drop to zero?

code.title: ReorderDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l01; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.IntConsumer; /** * The store-buffering test. Thread A runs {@code x = 1; r1 = y;} and thread B runs {@code y = 1; r2 = x;}. * If the four lines ran in any order that keeps each thread's two lines in program order, * at least one thread would read a 1. Count the trials where both threads read 0. */ public class ReorderDemo { static final class Plain { int x, y; } static final class Volatile { volatile int x, y; } static final int TRIALS = 1 << 19; static final int BATCH = 32; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int run = 1; run <= 3; run++) { System.out.printf("run %d: both read 0 in %,7d trials with plain fields, %,d with volatile fields (of %,d)%n", run, plain(), withVolatile(), TRIALS); } } static int plain() throws InterruptedException { Plain[] s = new Plain[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Plain(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } static int withVolatile() throws InterruptedException { Volatile[] s = new Volatile[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Volatile(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads. A small spin barrier every BATCH trials // keeps the two threads on the same trial at about the same moment. static void race(IntConsumer a, IntConsumer b) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger doneA = new AtomicInteger(), doneB = new AtomicInteger(); Thread ta = new Thread(() -> runSide(a, doneA, doneB)); Thread tb = new Thread(() -> runSide(b, doneB, doneA)); ta.start(); tb.start(); ta.join(); tb.join(); } static void runSide(IntConsumer side, AtomicInteger mine, AtomicInteger other) { for (int batch = 0; batch < TRIALS / BATCH; batch++) { mine.set(batch); while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait(); // wait for the other thread for (int i = batch * BATCH; i < (batch + 1) * BATCH; i++) side.accept(i); } } static int bothZero(int[] r1, int[] r2) { int n = 0; for (int i = 0; i < r1.length; i++) if (r1[i] == 0 && r2[i] == 0) n++; return n; } }

alt.title: ReorderDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.jmm.l01 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.function.IntConsumer import kotlin.concurrent.thread /* * The store-buffering test. Thread A runs `x = 1; r1 = y` and thread B runs `y = 1; r2 = x`. * If the four lines ran in any order that keeps each thread's two lines in program order, * at least one thread would read a 1. Count the trials where both threads read 0. */ private class PlainPair { var x = 0; var y = 0 } private class VolatilePair { @Volatile var x = 0; @Volatile var y = 0 } private const val TRIALS = 1 shl 19 private const val BATCH = 32 fun main() { for (run in 1..3) { println("run %d: both read 0 in %,7d trials with plain fields, %,d with @Volatile fields (of %,d)" .format(run, plain(), withVolatile(), TRIALS)) } } private fun plain(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { PlainPair() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } private fun withVolatile(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { VolatilePair() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads. A small spin barrier every BATCH trials // keeps the two threads on the same trial at about the same moment. private fun race(a: IntConsumer, b: IntConsumer) { val doneA = AtomicInteger() val doneB = AtomicInteger() val ta = thread { runSide(a, doneA, doneB) } val tb = thread { runSide(b, doneB, doneA) } ta.join(); tb.join() } private fun runSide(side: IntConsumer, mine: AtomicInteger, other: AtomicInteger) { for (batch in 0 until TRIALS / BATCH) { mine.set(batch) while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait() // wait for the other thread for (i in batch * BATCH until (batch + 1) * BATCH) side.accept(i) } } private fun bothZero(r1: IntArray, r2: IntArray): Int = r1.indices.count { r1[it] == 0 && r2[it] == 0 }

try.expect: With plain fields, a large share of trials see both reads return 0 (runs here showed between about 150,000 and 290,000 of 524,288, a different number every run). With volatile fields, the count is 0 every time. Under -Xint, the plain count drops but stays well above zero (44,000 to 110,000 here). The interpreter doesn't reorder anything, so those trials come from the store buffer, not the compiler.

video.title: Why the stop loop spins: the caches agree, the store buffer drains, the JIT keeps stop in a register

sections.h: Three layers that reorder your code, and the one contract above them
sections.html:
Three layers stand between the code you write and what other threads observe:

  • javac, the Java compiler, barely changes the order. It turns statements into bytecode almost one for one.
  • The JIT hoists reads out of loops, merges and drops writes, and swaps independent reads and writes. (HotSpot has two JIT compilers: C1 for code that runs often, and C2 for code that runs very often.)
  • The processor runs ahead through its store buffers, and ARM processors reorder more freely still.

Each layer follows the as-if-serial rule, so a single thread never notices. You can't control which layer does what, and you don't need to. The JMM is a contract that sits above all three. Think of it as the office rulebook: it says when a clerk is promised to see a colleague's note, whatever the desks and trays look like.

The contract names the operations that link threads: reads and writes of volatile fields, taking and releasing a lock, starting a thread and waiting for it with join(), and the classes in java.util.concurrent, the JDK's package of concurrency tools. Link every read of shared data to the write it needs, and your program behaves as if its lines ran one at a time, in the shuffled-decks order. That property is called sequential consistency, and the next lesson shows how the links work.

If you skip the links, you have a data race: two threads use the same variable, at least one of them writes it, and nothing links the two. Then the promises mostly go away. A thread can see an old value forever, or see a write without an earlier write that came before it. For long and double fields, it can even see half of one write and half of another.

Data races are why "it works on my machine" means so little here. Your test ran on one kind of processor, with one JIT, on a quiet day. A different JDK, a busier server or an ARM machine can show a reordering your tests never saw. Take a sample from jcstress, the tool from Testing and debugging that runs tiny tests millions of times. One thread writes x and then y, with the compiler told to keep that order, and another thread reads y and then x. On x86, seeing the new y with the old x never happened. On a 64-bit ARM machine, it happened in 0.68% of the samples. Both results obey the same JMM. Write to the contract, and the hardware becomes someone else's problem.

Your laptop doesn't decide what's correct; the memory model does. Write to the model.

Check yourself: you run StopFlagDemo with -Xint on an ARM laptop, which reorders more than x86. Does the worker stop? It does. The interpreter reads stop from memory on every pass, and coherence brings the new value to the worker's core. ARM's extra freedom only changes the order in which writes to different fields become visible, and each write still arrives. The plain field is still a data race, though, so the fix stays volatile.

We've seen one link, volatile, fix one loop. The rulebook has a whole chapter of them, and the next lesson reads it.

compare.title: A stop flag in Java and Kotlin

java.title: ReceiptPrinter.java
java.html: public class ReceiptPrinter implements Runnable { private volatile boolean running = true; @Override public void run() { while (running) { printNextReceipt(); } } public void stop() { running = false; } }

kotlin.title: ReceiptPrinter.kt
kotlin.html: class ReceiptPrinter : Runnable { @Volatile private var running = true override fun run() { while (running) { printNextReceipt() } } fun stop() { running = false } }

compare.note: Both classes are the same stop flag, and the Kotlin one is a direct translation. Kotlin has no volatile keyword. You put @Volatile on a var property, and the compiler marks its backing field (the JVM field that holds the value) volatile, so the bytecode matches the Java version. A val can't be @Volatile, because it's never written after construction. A plain Kotlin var has exactly the same bug as a plain Java field: while (running) compiles to a field read that the JIT can hoist. AtomicBoolean from java.util.concurrent.atomic works the same from both languages.

worked.title: Find the two flags that freeze a backup printer

steps.say: A shop's program has a backup helper that prints receipts only when the main printer breaks. A thread that watches the main printer calls takeOver() when it fails. When the program quits, a shutdown thread calls stop(). In a test, the main printer was unplugged. The backup was told to take over, printed nothing, and then ignored the request to quit as well. Find the shared state before you read on.
steps.code: class BackupPrinter implements Runnable { private boolean onDuty; // 1. written by the thread that watches the main printer private boolean running = true; // 2. written by the shutdown thread @Override public void run() { while (running) { // 3. both flags read in a busy loop if (onDuty) printNext(); } } void takeOver() { onDuty = true; } void stop() { running = false; } }

alt.html: class BackupPrinter : Runnable { private var onDuty = false // 1. written by the thread that watches the main printer private var running = true // 2. written by the shutdown thread override fun run() { while (running) { // 3. both flags read in a busy loop if (onDuty) printNext() } } fun takeOver() { onDuty = true } fun stop() { running = false } }

steps.say: Both flags are written by one thread and read by another, and nothing links them. While the main printer works, onDuty stays false for hours. The JIT keeps a profile, a record of which branches the running code takes. It sees that printNext() never runs, and compiles the loop as if that branch weren't there. What's left is two reads of plain fields that nothing in the loop writes, so it reads each one once. A copy of this class, run for this lesson on JDK 21 and on JDK 25, printed 0 receipts in the second after takeOver(). It was still spinning 3 seconds after stop().
Make both flags volatile. Then stop the backup from spinning: while it has nothing to do, it can sleep between checks and leave the core to other work.
steps.code: class BackupPrinter implements Runnable { private volatile boolean onDuty; // 1. both flags cross threads: both volatile private volatile boolean running = true; @Override public void run() { try { while (running) { // 2. read again on every pass if (onDuty) { printNext(); } else { Thread.sleep(50); // 3. a backup on standby doesn't need a whole core } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // 4. treat an interrupt as a stop, too } } void takeOver() { onDuty = true; } void stop() { running = false; } }

alt.html: class BackupPrinter : Runnable { @Volatile private var onDuty = false // 1. both flags cross threads: both @Volatile @Volatile private var running = true override fun run() { try { while (running) { // 2. read again on every pass if (onDuty) { printNext() } else { Thread.sleep(50) // 3. a backup on standby doesn't need a whole core } } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // 4. treat an interrupt as a stop, too } } fun takeOver() { onDuty = true } fun stop() { running = false } }

steps.say: The sleep alone would also have hidden the hang, because HotSpot reads fields again after it. That's exactly why the volatile stays. The sleep is there to save the processor's time. The volatile is there for correctness, and it keeps working after the next change to the loop.

lab.title: Unhang a work loop and a board of exchange rates
steps: Meet the two classes. SettlementLoop is a helper that runs passes of work in a loop (settling, in bank talk, means closing out the day's payments) until another thread calls stop(). FxRateBoard holds today's exchange rates, what one currency costs in another, like the board at an airport exchange desk. A loader thread fills it once at startup, and request threads wait in awaitRates() until the rates are in.
Run the tests once. Two of the three fail with "still spinning" or "still waiting". Each failing test waits 5 seconds for a thread that never finishes, so the run takes a little while.
Fix SettlementLoop with the smallest change that lets the write in stop() reach the loop. Run the tests.
In FxRateBoard, first try making only rates volatile, and run the tests. Predict whether they pass, then see.
Now fix the field that matters, and leave the other one plain. Run the tests three times in a row.
hints: The tests sleep 300 ms before calling stop() or publish(). That gives the JIT time to compile the spinning loop, which is the moment the plain field gets read once and never again.
awaitRates() spins on ready, not on rates. The field the loop reads is the one the JIT can hoist.
Why may rates stay plain? It is written before the volatile write to ready, and read after the volatile read sees true. Happens-before, the next lesson, names that rule.
Adding Thread.onSpinWait() or a log call to the loop may make a test pass on HotSpot. That's the lucky accident from section 2. Fix the field instead.
lab.done: All three tests in VisibilityTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A worker that is sure to stop
drill.prompt: Close this page. From memory, write a class Poller implements Runnable whose run() keeps calling pollOnce() until another thread calls shutdown(). It must be sure to stop. Then write one sentence on why a plain boolean is not enough.

answer.html: public class Poller implements Runnable { private volatile boolean running = true; // volatile: the loop reads it every pass, and the write is visible @Override public void run() { while (running) { pollOnce(); } } public void shutdown() { running = false; } private void pollOnce() { /* do one small job */ } } // With a plain boolean, nothing links the write in shutdown() to the read in run(), // so the JIT may read the field once and loop forever.

alt.html: class Poller : Runnable { @Volatile private var running = true // @Volatile: the loop reads it every pass, and the write is visible override fun run() { while (running) { pollOnce() } } fun shutdown() { running = false } private fun pollOnce() { /* do one small job */ } } // With a plain var, nothing links the write in shutdown() to the read in run(), // so the JIT may read the field once and loop forever.

recap: A loop on a plain field can spin forever: the JIT may read the field once and keep it in a register, the core's private notepad.
The hang goes away under -Xint, which turns the JIT off. So it comes from the compiler, not from the caches.
Caches are coherent: a write crosses out every other copy within nanoseconds. Store buffers let a core's later read pass its own earlier write, so other threads can see the two swapped.

Each layer (javac, the JIT, the processor) may reorder as long as one thread alone can't tell. Other threads can tell. sleep, yield, log lines and onSpinWait hide the bug on today's HotSpot and promise nothing.
Correctness comes from the JMM, not from your processor: code that passes on x86 can fail on ARM.
The limit: volatile fixed one flag. Which operations link threads in general, and how far each link reaches, is the subject of happens-before, next.

explain.prompt: A friend says: "The stop flag works when I step through it in the debugger, so it can't be a visibility bug." Explain, in your own words, why it hangs in a real run and what the fix is.
explain.answer: In the debugger the code runs slowly, often in the interpreter, so every pass of the loop reads the field from memory and sees the new value. In a real run the loop gets busy and the JIT compiles it. The field is plain and nothing in the loop links the threads, so the compiler may read it once and keep the value in a register. The CPU caches are not the problem; they stay in agreement. The fix is to make the flag volatile, or an AtomicBoolean. Then the JIT must read it on every pass, and the memory model promises that the write from the other thread becomes visible.

deeper.html:
volatile is the usual fix, but it does more than this loop needs. The weakest tool that already promises the loop will end is opaque access (getOpaque and setOpaque, JDK 9 and later). It goes through a VarHandle, an object that reads and writes a field with a strength you choose. The jcstress sample BasicJMM_04_Progress makes the point. For the plain spin loop, "Test is stuck" is listed as an allowed result. The volatile spin loop finished in every one of the 17,882 runs the sample records. For the opaque spin loop, getting stuck is marked forbidden. Opaque stops the compiler from keeping the read on its notepad and leaves the rest to the hardware, which makes every write visible sooner or later. It doesn't order other fields, which is why it's rarely what you want. VarHandles and memory ordering modes, the last lesson of this track, covers the modes.

The sample BasicJMM_06_Causality is the cleanest look at hardware differences. One thread writes x = 1 then y = 1, and another reads y then x. With plain fields, the sample's recorded run saw y == 1 but x == 0 in 0.09% of samples. With opaque accesses, which keep the compiler from reordering, x86 showed it 0 times, because x86 keeps writes in order. A 64-bit ARM machine still showed it in 0.68% of samples. Make y volatile and that result is forbidden on every platform.

If you want the long version of why the JMM is written as a contract about whole runs of a program, read Aleksey Shipilëv's "Java Memory Model Pragmatics". It is long, and worth one slow evening.
